explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend, but the man says the opposite. He asks the LORD, "Do not hide Your face from me in my day of distress," and then adds, "answer me quickly when I call." That's a man who needs help NOW, not one who wants God to check His schedule.

That's right. He asks God to "answer me quickly when I call." He's in a day of distress, and he asks the LORD not to hide His face from him. Nobody in that spot says, "No rush, whenever you get to it."
Yes, friend. Smoke doesn't stay put. You try to grab it and your hand comes back empty. He says his days "vanish like smoke," and I think he's saying his life feels like it's disappearing on him.

I get it, smoke does drift off. But the man says his days vanish, not his troubles. Right after that he says his bones burn like glowing embers, so nothing in these lines says the hard stuff is blowing over.

Smoke can cloud up a room, so I see the thinking. But the man doesn't say his mind is foggy. He says his days vanish like smoke, and vanishing is about something going away, not something getting murky.
That's it. He says, "I even forget to eat my bread." Bread is right there and he still doesn't touch it. The man is carrying something heavy, and the verse shows it.
Sharing bread is a good thing, friend, but that's not what he says. The verse says he forgets to eat his bread. It's about what his affliction does to him, not about what he gives away.
Blessing the bread sounds like a fine mealtime habit, but it isn't in this verse. He says he even forgets to eat it. His heart is afflicted and withered like grass, and eating drops off the list.

Right on. A desert owl, an owl among the ruins, a lone bird on a housetop: every picture is a creature by itself with nobody around. He's lying awake while he says it. I bet it's a long, quiet night for him.

A bird on a rooftop might sound peaceful, friend, but the man's words point the other way. He's an owl among ruins and a bird that's all alone. He says he lies awake, and that doesn't sound like a man resting easy.

explanations.answer: He feels ready to fly home
explanations.explanation: Birds do fly, so I see the pull of that one. But the man never says anything about home or flying off. He just sits there, a lone bird on a housetop, and that picture is about being by himself.
Yes, friend. He says, "All day long my enemies taunt me." All day, not just once in a while. It's a long stretch to carry that on top of feeling alone.
This one is in the text, friend. Verse 8 says, "All day long my enemies taunt me; they ridicule me and curse me." So the man is feeling alone and getting taunted at the same time.

That's what he says. He eats ashes like bread and mixes his drink with tears "because of Your indignation and wrath." He's talking straight to the LORD when he says it. It's a heavy verse, so I'll just let it sit there.

I see why that might come to mind, but the man doesn't say it. He names the LORD's indignation and wrath as the reason for his ashes and tears. He never lists his own sin here, so I won't add it for him.

A hungry land would explain the bread trouble, but no famine shows up in this prayer. The man says his sorrow comes "because of Your indignation and wrath." Drought isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses.

Yes, friend. When the sun gets low, shadows stretch out long, and that tells you the day is winding down. I think that's the feeling he's after. His days are getting long shadows and he's withering away like grass.

Morning shadows can stretch out long too, so good eye. But a morning is a day just getting started, and this man says his days are withering away like grass. Evening fits better, with the day wearing out.

At noon the sun is high overhead and shadows are at their SHORTEST, friend. The man says his days are like lengthening shadows, so they're getting longer, not shorter. That points to the day running low, not the middle of it.

That's the turn. The man says, "But You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever." His own days are fading like shadows, and he looks up at the One whose throne doesn't fade. That's a lot of comfort packed into a few words.

explanations.answer: He is far off and silent
explanations.explanation: I can see why, since the man started out begging God not to hide His face. But after the "But," he says the LORD "sit[s] enthroned forever." He doesn't call Him far off or silent anywhere in this verse.

explanations.answer: He has grown tired of Zion
explanations.explanation: Not at all, friend. Verse 13 says the LORD "will rise up and have compassion on Zion." The man isn't saying God is tired of her. He says God is about to show her compassion.
I see the thinking, but the man says the opposite. He says it is time to show Zion favor, and that "the appointed time has come." So there's no long wait in that verse.
That's right. The man tells the LORD, "for it is time to show her favor," and says the appointed time has come. The waiting part is over in his prayer.
Yes, friend. The man says, "So the nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear Your glory." Nations and kings, the whole lineup. It's a big picture.
This one is right there in verse 15. The man says, "So the nations will fear the name of the LORD." He adds that all the kings of the earth will fear God's glory too.
Yes, rebuild. The man says, "For the LORD will rebuild Zion." Her stones and her dust matter to God's servants, and the LORD is the one who builds her back up.
That would be a sad turn, friend, but it's not what the man says. He says the LORD "will rebuild Zion," and he adds that the LORD has appeared in His glory. Abandoning her isn't in the verse.

Judging could sound like a natural next step, but the verse says something else. The man says the LORD "will rebuild Zion." Right after God's servants pity her dust, he looks ahead to her being built up again.

I get why you'd pick it, but the verse says the opposite. The man says the LORD "will turn toward the prayer of the destitute; He will not despise their prayer." Not despise, friend. That's good news for anyone who feels down to their last crumb.
That's right. Verse 17 says, "He will turn toward the prayer of the destitute; He will not despise their prayer." The LORD turns toward those prayers, and He doesn't look down on them.

explanations.answer: So future people can praise the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. "Let this be written for the generation to come, so that a people not yet created may praise the LORD." He's writing for people who haven't even been born yet. I think that's a generous thing to do.

explanations.answer: So future people can remember him
explanations.explanation: The man doesn't ask to be remembered, friend. The reason in verse 18 is that a people not yet created may praise the LORD. His name never comes up as the point.

explanations.answer: So future people can avoid his trouble
explanations.explanation: A warning label would make sense in a lot of stories, but this verse doesn't give that reason. The man says it's written so that a people not yet created may praise the LORD. Praise is the reason on the page.
Yes, friend. The text says the LORD gazed out from heaven to earth "to hear a prisoner's groaning." God looked down to listen to someone who was groaning, and that's the whole picture.
Songs are a nice thought, but verse 20 doesn't say that. The LORD looked down "to hear a prisoner's groaning." The nations come up in verse 15, but not as what He listened for here.
Nothing in these verses has God listening for boasting. He looked down "to hear a prisoner's groaning." That's a much quieter sound than a boast, and He heard it anyway.

That's the word. The LORD looked down "to hear a prisoner's groaning, to release those condemned to death." Hearing the groan and releasing the prisoner go together in this verse, and I think that's beautiful.
I see why that word might come to mind with a prisoner involved. But the verse says the LORD looked down "to release those condemned to death." Release, not judge, friend.
A warning is a fair guess, but it isn't what the man says. The verse says the LORD gazed down "to release those condemned to death." The LORD's aim there is setting them free.

explanations.answer: Not to take him in the midst of his days
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. He says, "O my God, do not take me in the midst of my days!" His strength is broken and his days are cut short, and he asks God for more time. I think you can hear how much he means it.

explanations.answer: To take him home right away
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what he asks. The man says, "do not take me in the midst of my days!" He wants more days, not fewer.

explanations.answer: To send his enemies far away
explanations.explanation: His enemies showed up back in verse 8, friend, but they aren't part of this request. In verse 24 he says, "O my God, do not take me in the midst of my days!" His ask is about his own days.

explanations.answer: They will perish and wear out
explanations.explanation: Right. The man says, "They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment." Even the heavens and the earth wear out like old clothes. And then comes the but: God remains.
Forever belongs to the LORD in this verse, friend. The man says of the earth and heavens, "They will perish, but You remain." The one who stays is God.

Hidden away isn't in the verse. The man says they "will perish" and "will all wear out like a garment." That's a much plainer picture of something wearing out, like a favorite apron after too many batches.
I get why you might guess that after all the hard words, but the prayer ends the other way. The man says, "The children of Your servants will dwell securely." Secure, friend, not scared.

That's right. The prayer ends with, "The children of Your servants will dwell securely, and their descendants will be established before You." After all those hard verses, it lands on safe and steady.
